questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman is diagnosed with stage 4 pancreatic cancer. She has no significant medical history and is concerned about how her immune system became so weak. Her oncologist explains that the tumor secretes a cytokine in large quantities that broadly suppresses the activity of B cells, T cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages. Which of the following substances is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: TGF-beta is a potent immunosuppressant cytokine that some tumors secrete to downregulate multiple immune lineages.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that TGF-beta is a potent immunosuppressant capable of suppressing the activities of B cells, T cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages, and that some tumor cells secrete it in large quantities to suppress the immune system.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FasL is a cell-surface protein that binds the Fas receptor on T cells to trigger apoptosis of cytotoxic T cells; it is not a secreted immunosuppressive cytokine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycocalyx is extracellular matrix material that masks surface antigens, not a cytokine that suppresses immune lineages.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interleukin-2 promotes T cell proliferation and activation, the opposite of immunosuppression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TNF-alpha causes cachexia in malignancy and recruits white blood cells rather than broadly suppressing immune cells.

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms allows tumor cells to evade immune detection specifically by masking their surface antigens?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of MHC class I molecules

explanation.summary: Antigen masking occurs when tumor cells coat themselves in excess extracellular matrix (glycocalyx).
explanation.whyCorrect: Many tumor cells secrete an excess of extracellular matrix material called glycocalyx. This thick coating masks the antigens on cancer cells, making it more difficult for immune cells to target them for destruction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Downregulating antigen expression is the outgrowth-of-antigen-variants mechanism, in which the antigen is lost rather than hidden.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of MHC class I removes the platform that displays antigen to cytotoxic T cells; it does not mask antigens with a coating.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TGF-beta secretion broadly suppresses immune cells and does not physically mask antigens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PD-L1 upregulation engages the PD-1 checkpoint to inhibit T cells rather than masking antigens.

questions.stem: A tumor subclone continues to display abundant tumor antigen, yet cytotoxic CD8+ T cells can no longer recognize or kill it. Analysis shows the cells have acquired a mutation that eliminates a surface receptor normally present on all nucleated cells. Loss of which of the following molecules best explains this finding?

explanation.summary: Cytotoxic T cells identify targets via MHC class I; tumor loss of MHC class I prevents recognition.
explanation.whyCorrect: MHC class I is a receptor present on all cells that displays antigens on the cell surface. Some tumor subclones undergo mutations that cause loss of MHC molecules so they are no longer recognized by cytotoxic T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B7 molecules are co-stimulatory ligands on antigen-presenting cells; they are not present on all nucleated cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD28 is a co-stimulatory receptor on T cells, not a molecule tumor cells lose to escape recognition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The Fas receptor is on T cells and mediates apoptosis when engaged by tumor FasL; losing it would not affect antigen recognition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PD-1 is an inhibitory receptor on T cells, not a molecule displayed on tumor cells for recognition.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced lung cancer that has failed multiple rounds of chemotherapy is started on pembrolizumab (Keytruda). Which of the following best describes how this medication helps the immune system attack the tumor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It engineers the patient's T cells to target CD19

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is an antibody that binds PD-1 on T cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: It neutralizes secreted TGF-beta in the tumor microenvironment

choices.label: D
choices.text: It restores MHC class I expression on tumor cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It supplies excess co-stimulatory signal directly to tumor cells

explanation.summary: Pembrolizumab is an anti-PD-1 antibody that blocks the inhibitory PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cancer cells upregulate PD-L1 and PD-L2, which activate the PD-1 receptor on T cells and suppress them. Keytruda is an antibody that binds the PD-1 receptor on T cells, preventing it from interacting with PD-L1 on cancer cells, giving the immune system a fighting chance to eliminate the tumor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Engineering T cells to target CD19 describes CAR-T cell therapy, not a PD-1 antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutralizing TGF-beta is a different immunosuppression pathway and is not the mechanism of pembrolizumab.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pembrolizumab does not alter MHC class I expression on tumor cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The drug does not deliver co-stimulation to tumor cells; it removes an inhibitory checkpoint signal.

questions.stem: A tumor is found to upregulate an inhibitory receptor that binds the B7 molecules on antigen-presenting cells and thereby reduces engagement of the CD28 co-stimulatory receptor on T cells. Which of the following molecules is being upregulated?

explanation.summary: CTLA-4 competes with CD28 for B7 ligands, dampening T cell co-stimulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cancer cells can upregulate the inhibitory receptor CTLA-4, which binds its ligands, the B7 molecules, from antigen-presenting cells and reduces the engagement of the CD28 co-stimulatory receptor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: FasL binds the Fas receptor to induce T cell apoptosis and has no role in B7/CD28 competition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MHC class II presents antigen to helper T cells and is not an inhibitory receptor for B7.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PD-L1 engages the PD-1 receptor on T cells; it does not bind B7 or block CD28.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TGF-beta is a secreted immunosuppressive cytokine, not a receptor that competes for B7.

questions.stem: A melanoma expresses a cell-surface ligand that engages a death receptor on approaching cytotoxic T cells, causing those T cells to die via the extrinsic apoptosis pathway. Which of the following ligands is the tumor most likely expressing?

explanation.summary: Tumors such as melanoma and hepatocellular carcinoma express FasL, which triggers extrinsic-pathway apoptosis of cytotoxic T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tumor cells such as melanoma and hepatocellular carcinoma express FasL, which binds the Fas receptor on T cells, leading to apoptosis of cytotoxic T cells via the extrinsic pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B7-1 is a co-stimulatory ligand that promotes T cell activation, not death.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD28 is a co-stimulatory receptor on T cells, not a tumor ligand that induces apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glycocalyx is a physical coating that masks antigens and does not engage a death receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PD-L2 engages PD-1 to inhibit T cells but does not directly trigger extrinsic-pathway apoptosis through a death receptor.

questions.stem: A T cell encounters a tumor cell that presents antigen through MHC but fails to deliver a co-stimulatory second signal. Which of the following is the most likely fate of this T cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It becomes anergic or undergoes apoptosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: It differentiates into a memory T cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: It proliferates into an activated effector clone

choices.label: D
choices.text: It secretes large amounts of TGF-beta

choices.label: E
choices.text: It upregulates MHC class I on the tumor cell

explanation.summary: T cells require two signals; antigen without co-stimulation leads to anergy or apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: A T cell can only be activated after receiving two signals: antigen recognition (Signal 1) and a co-stimulatory signal from the antigen-presenting cell (Signal 2). If the co-stimulatory signal is not received, the T cell becomes unresponsive (anergic) or undergoes apoptosis, which tumor cells exploit to evade immunity.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Memory differentiation follows productive activation, which does not occur without Signal 2.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Effector proliferation requires both signals; without co-stimulation the T cell is not activated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TGF-beta is secreted by tumor cells, not by T cells lacking co-stimulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A T cell does not restore MHC class I on the tumor cell; MHC expression is a tumor property.

questions.stem: A patient with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma initially responds to CAR-T cell therapy engineered against CD19, but later relapses. Biopsy of the recurrent tumor shows the malignant B cells no longer express CD19. Which of the following best explains the relapse?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The engineered T cells lost their MHC class I molecules

choices.label: B
choices.text: The engineered T cells were suppressed by CD28 co-stimulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: The tumor cells began secreting glycocalyx to physically block the CAR-T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: The tumor cells lost expression of the target antigen

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tumor cells upregulated MHC class I to hide from the CAR-T cells

explanation.summary: Antigen escape occurs when tumor cells stop expressing the CAR-T target (CD19).
explanation.whyCorrect: In CAR-T therapy the patient's own T cells are engineered to target a specific antigen such as CD19 on B cells. A well-known challenge is that cancer cells may stop expressing CD19 on their surface, so there is no longer a target for the engineered T cells, allowing relapse.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CAR-T cells recognize CD19 directly and do not depend on tumor MHC; loss of the T cells' own MHC does not explain relapse.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD28 co-stimulation promotes, rather than suppresses, T cell activity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The biopsy shows loss of CD19, not a glycocalyx coating, as the cause.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CAR-T recognition of CD19 is MHC-independent, so upregulating MHC class I would not hide the tumor from CAR-T cells.

questions.stem: In a melanoma, highly immunogenic tumor subclones are eliminated by the host immune system, while other subclones that have lost or downregulated their surface antigens survive and expand. Which mechanism of immune evasion does this describe?

explanation.summary: Selective survival of antigen-negative subclones is the outgrowth of antigen variants.
explanation.whyCorrect: If a subclone is highly immunogenic it is eliminated, whereas some tumor subclones lose expression of a surface antigen or downregulate antigen expression so they are not recognized by immune cells. This has been observed in cancers such as melanoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antigen masking hides antigens under a glycocalyx coat; here the antigens are actually lost, not covered.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PD-L1 checkpoint engagement inhibits T cells directly and does not describe subclone selection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TGF-beta immunosuppression is cytokine-mediated and does not involve selection of antigen-negative subclones.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lack of co-stimulation causes T cell anergy/apoptosis and is distinct from loss of tumor antigen.

questions.stem: A medical student reads that a normal function of the immune system is to constantly scan the body for emerging malignant cells and destroy them, and that avoiding this process is one of the hallmarks of cancer. This normal protective function is best described by which of the following terms?

explanation.summary: Immune surveillance is the immune system's continuous scanning for and destruction of malignant cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The term immune surveillance implies that a normal function of the immune system is to constantly scan the body for emerging malignant cells and destroy them; avoiding immune destruction is one of the hallmarks of cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anergy is an unresponsive state of T cells that lack co-stimulation, not immune scanning.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antigen masking is a tumor evasion strategy, not a normal immune function.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cachexia is the wasting syndrome associated with TNF-alpha in malignancy, unrelated to immune scanning.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Checkpoint blockade is a therapy that uses antibodies against CTLA-4 and PD-L1, not the normal scanning function.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced malignancy develops profound weight loss and muscle wasting. A cytokine elevated in this patient is known to cause cachexia in malignancy and to recruit white blood cells, and it is distinct from the immunosuppressive cytokine that tumors use to evade immunity. Which of the following cytokines is most likely responsible for the wasting?

explanation.summary: TNF-alpha causes cachexia in malignancy and recruits white blood cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that TNF-alpha causes cachexia in malignancy and leads to white blood cell recruitment, distinguishing it from TGF-beta, the immunosuppressant tumors secrete to evade immunity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FasL is a death-inducing surface ligand that triggers T cell apoptosis, not a cause of cachexia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Interleukin-2 activates and expands T cells and does not cause cachexia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PD-L1 is a checkpoint ligand on tumor cells, not a cytokine that causes wasting.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TGF-beta is the immunosuppressive cytokine that downregulates immune lineages; it is not the cause of cachexia described here.

questions.stem: A newer class of cancer therapy, described as checkpoint blockade, uses antibodies to restore T cell function against tumors. Against which of the following pairs of targets are these checkpoint-blockade antibodies directed?

choices.label: D
choices.text: MHC class I and MHC class II

explanation.summary: Checkpoint blockade uses antibodies against CTLA-4 and PD-L1 to restore T cell function.
explanation.whyCorrect: New cancer therapy known as checkpoint blockade uses antibodies against CTLA-4 and PD-L1 to restore T cell function; it is now approved for advanced-stage solid tumors and some forms of lymphoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD28 and B7 are activating co-stimulatory molecules; blocking them would suppress, not restore, T cell function.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fas and FasL mediate apoptosis and are not the targets of approved checkpoint-blockade therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MHC class I and II present antigen and are not the targets of checkpoint-blockade antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TGF-beta and TNF-alpha are cytokines and are not the checkpoint targets named for this therapy.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to a dermatology clinic with extensive freckling over the face and neck but very few freckles on the shoulders. He develops severe sunburn after only a few minutes of sun exposure, and two lesions removed from his face were squamous cell carcinomas. A defect in which of the following DNA repair mechanisms most likely underlies his condition?

explanation.summary: Xeroderma pigmentosum results from a defect in nucleotide excision repair (NER).
explanation.whyCorrect: The photosensitivity, freckling limited to sun-exposed areas, and early squamous cell carcinomas describe xeroderma pigmentosum, caused by inherited loss-of-function of NER. NER normally removes and replaces oligonucleotides containing UV-induced pyrimidine dimers, and because humans lack photolyase, NER is the key mechanism for repairing this damage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick attributes this photosensitive skin-cancer syndrome to defective nucleotide excision repair, not base excision repair.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Defective homologous recombination underlies BRCA1/2-associated breast and ovarian cancers, not xeroderma pigmentosum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Defective mismatch repair causes Lynch syndrome with gastrointestinal and endometrial cancer, not photosensitive skin cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Defective nonhomologous end joining is linked to severe combined immunodeficiency and ataxia telangiectasia.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is diagnosed with an adenocarcinoma of the cecum. His mother and a maternal uncle had colorectal cancer, and a sister had endometrial cancer, with several relatives diagnosed before age 50. Molecular testing of the tumor shows microsatellite instability. A defect in which of the following processes is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Lynch syndrome is caused by defective mismatch repair, producing microsatellite instability.
explanation.whyCorrect: The family pattern of colorectal and endometrial cancer with early onset, plus microsatellite instability, indicates Lynch syndrome. Defective mismatch repair fails to correct replication errors, so microsatellites (tandem repeats of 1-6 nucleotides) become unstable in length.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Direct reversal is not the pathway the brick links to microsatellite instability or Lynch syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Defective homologous recombination is associated with BRCA-related breast and ovarian cancer, not microsatellite instability.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Defective nonhomologous end joining causes immunodeficiency and ataxia telangiectasia, not this colorectal cancer syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Defective nucleotide excision repair causes xeroderma pigmentosum, a UV-sensitive skin disorder.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with a strong family history of breast and ovarian cancer is found to carry a germline BRCA1 mutation. The protein encoded by this gene normally participates in which of the following DNA repair processes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Homologous recombination repair of double-strand breaks

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mismatch repair of errors made during replication

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nonhomologous end joining of broken double-strand DNA ends

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nucleotide excision repair of ultraviolet pyrimidine dimers

choices.label: E
choices.text: Proofreading of new strands by DNA polymerase

explanation.summary: BRCA1 functions in homologous recombination repair of double-strand breaks.
explanation.whyCorrect: Individuals with BRCA1 mutations have defective homologous recombination and are at elevated risk of breast and ovarian cancer. Homologous recombination uses a homologous chromosome as a template to accurately repair double-strand breaks without loss of nucleotides.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mismatch repair defects cause Lynch syndrome, not BRCA-associated cancers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nonhomologous end joining directly fuses DNA ends without homology and is not the BRCA1 pathway; its defects cause immunodeficiency and ataxia telangiectasia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nucleotide excision repair addresses helix-distorting lesions such as UV pyrimidine dimers, and its defect causes xeroderma pigmentosum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Polymerase proofreading is a replication fidelity function, not the homologous recombination role of BRCA1.

questions.stem: A young child has a history of severe combined immunodeficiency and later develops gait ataxia, choreoathetosis, and dilated blood vessels visible in the conjunctivae and skin. A defect in which of the following DNA repair mechanisms best explains this combination of findings?

explanation.summary: Defective nonhomologous end joining underlies both severe combined immunodeficiency and ataxia telangiectasia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nonhomologous end joining is normally harnessed during V(D)J recombination in B cells; its defects can cause severe combined immunodeficiency. The brick also lists ataxia telangiectasia, with ataxia and telangiectasias of skin and eyes, as a clinical consequence of defective NHEJ.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Base excision repair is not the pathway the brick associates with these findings.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Defective homologous recombination causes BRCA-related cancers and Fanconi anemia, not this immunodeficiency-plus-ataxia picture.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Defective mismatch repair causes Lynch syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Defective nucleotide excision repair causes xeroderma pigmentosum.

questions.stem: Immunohistochemical staining of a colorectal tumor shows loss of MLH1 and PMS2 nuclear staining in the malignant glands, while MSH2 and MSH6 staining remain intact. This pattern most strongly indicates a primary defect in which of the following genes?

explanation.summary: Simultaneous loss of MLH1 and PMS2 points to a primary MLH1 defect.
explanation.whyCorrect: MLH1 and PMS2 form a functional heterodimer, so a defect in MLH1 destabilizes and leads to loss of PMS2 as well. Seeing both proteins absent therefore indicates a primary problem with the MLH1 gene.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BRCA1 acts in homologous recombination and is unrelated to this mismatch repair immunohistochemistry pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MSH2 staining is intact, so it is not the defective gene.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PMS2 is lost secondarily because it is destabilized when its MLH1 partner is defective, so it is not the primary problem here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MSH6 staining is intact, so it is not the defective gene.

questions.stem: A pathology report on a colon cancer notes that tandem repeats of 1-6 nucleotides scattered throughout the tumor genome have become unstable and vary in length compared with normal tissue. This finding is a direct hallmark of a defect in which of the following?

explanation.summary: Microsatellite instability is a hallmark of defective mismatch repair.
explanation.whyCorrect: Microsatellites are tandem repeats of 1-6 nucleotides whose length normally stays constant. When mismatch repair is defective, these repeats become unstable and change in length, a state termed microsatellite instability.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Homologous recombination defects cause BRCA-related and Fanconi phenotypes, not microsatellite instability.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nonhomologous end joining defects cause immunodeficiency and translocations, not microsatellite length changes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nucleotide excision repair defects cause xeroderma pigmentosum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Telomerase maintains chromosome ends and is unrelated to microsatellite instability.

questions.stem: A physician is evaluating a family for possible Lynch syndrome. Which of the following findings would be most suspicious for the diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A family history limited to pancreatic cancer in three relatives of a single generation

choices.label: B
choices.text: An isolated case of childhood leukemia in one relative of a single generation

choices.label: C
choices.text: At least three relatives with breast cancer only, spanning two successive generations of the family

choices.label: D
choices.text: At least three relatives with colorectal or endometrial cancer across two successive generations

choices.label: E
choices.text: One relative in a single generation diagnosed with colorectal cancer after age 70

explanation.summary: Lynch syndrome is suggested by multiple relatives with colorectal or endometrial cancer, successive generations, and early onset.
explanation.whyCorrect: Clinical signs of possible Lynch syndrome include at least three relatives with a Lynch-associated cancer such as colorectal or endometrial cancer (one a first-degree relative of the other two), at least two successive generations affected, and at least one diagnosed before age 50.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A family history of only pancreatic cancer is not immediately suspicious for Lynch syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Isolated childhood leukemia is not part of the Lynch syndrome clinical criteria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The prototypical cancers are colorectal and endometrial, not breast cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Colorectal cancer diagnosed after age 70 is less likely to be inherited; early onset (before 50) is more suspicious.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child has short stature, absent thumbs and other skeletal abnormalities, and progressive pancytopenia. Cultured cells show marked chromosomal breakage when exposed to diepoxybutane, and the condition is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. A defect in which of the following repair processes best explains this disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Homologous recombination repair of DNA cross-links

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mismatch repair of base-base replication errors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nonhomologous end joining of broken DNA ends

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nucleotide excision repair of ultraviolet pyrimidine dimers

choices.label: E
choices.text: Proofreading by DNA polymerase during replication

explanation.summary: Fanconi anemia results from defective homologous recombination repair of DNA cross-links.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fanconi anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in genes encoding proteins that repair DNA cross-links through homologous recombination. It is characterized by developmental abnormalities such as short stature and skeletal defects, hypersensitivity to cross-linking agents, bone marrow failure, and increased leukemia risk.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mismatch repair defects cause Lynch syndrome, not this marrow failure syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nonhomologous end joining defects cause immunodeficiency and ataxia telangiectasia, not cross-link hypersensitivity with marrow failure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nucleotide excision repair defects cause xeroderma pigmentosum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Polymerase proofreading is a replication fidelity mechanism, not the cross-link repair pathway defective in Fanconi anemia.

questions.stem: Nucleotide excision repair is described as particularly important for correcting ultraviolet-light-induced pyrimidine dimers in humans. Which of the following best explains why humans rely on NER for this purpose?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pyrimidine dimers are repaired only during mitosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pyrimidine dimers cannot be recognized by any repair system

explanation.summary: Humans lack photolyase, so NER is the key mechanism for repairing UV pyrimidine dimers.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that because humans lack photolyase, NER is an important mechanism to repair pyrimidine dimers. NER recognizes the helix-distorting dimer and removes and replaces the oligonucleotide containing it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Humans have DNA ligase, which in fact seals the gap during NER.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of proofreading is not the reason NER is needed for UV dimers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick does not restrict pyrimidine dimer repair to mitosis; the point is the absence of photolyase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyrimidine dimers are recognized precisely by NER as helix-distorting lesions.

questions.stem: The error-prone nature of nonhomologous end joining, which can fuse any two DNA ends without requiring homology, is physiologically harnessed by the immune system for which of the following processes?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Somatic mismatch repair in T cells

explanation.summary: NHEJ is used physiologically for V(D)J recombination to generate antibody and receptor diversity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that the inaccuracy of NHEJ has physiological utility, allowing B cells to undergo V(D)J recombination, the process by which novel antibodies and receptors are generated to detect foreign antigens. This is why NHEJ defects can cause severe combined immunodeficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Meiotic recombination uses homologous recombination, not the error-prone NHEJ pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nucleotide excision repair is unrelated to immune receptor diversity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: V(D)J recombination, not mismatch repair, is the NHEJ-dependent immune process described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Telomere elongation depends on telomerase, not NHEJ.

questions.stem: During a review of genomic instability, a student is asked to name the most commonly mutated gene in cancer, often called the guardian of the genome. Which of the following is the correct answer?

explanation.summary: TP53 (p53) is the most commonly mutated gene in cancer and is called the guardian of the genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's review prompt identifies the most commonly mutated gene in cancer, also known as the guardian of the genome, as p53 (TP53). It guards genomic integrity by halting the cell cycle for repair or triggering apoptosis when damage is excessive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BRCA1 mutations cause defective homologous recombination and breast/ovarian cancer but are not the guardian of the genome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MLH1 is a mismatch repair gene linked to Lynch syndrome, not the guardian of the genome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MSH2 is a mismatch repair gene involved in Lynch syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PMS2 is a mismatch repair gene, lost secondarily with MLH1, not the guardian of the genome.

questions.stem: A cell in late S/G2 phase sustains a double-strand DNA break and has an intact, undamaged copy of the same sequence available. It repairs the break by reconnecting the complementary strands without the loss of any nucleotide sequence. Which of the following repair mechanisms was used, and why is it favored over the alternative?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Base excision repair, because it excises a single damaged base without losing sequence

choices.label: B
choices.text: Homologous recombination, because it uses a homologous chromosome as a template

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mismatch repair, because it corrects errors left behind by replication

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nonhomologous end joining, because it never introduces mutations at the break

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nucleotide excision repair, because it removes bulky helix-distorting adducts

explanation.summary: Homologous recombination accurately repairs double-strand breaks using a homologous chromosome as template.
explanation.whyCorrect: Homologous recombination uses a homologous chromosome as a template to reconnect severed strands without loss of nucleotide sequence, making it the accurate double-strand break repair pathway. It is preferred over nonhomologous end joining, which is error-prone and can even cause chromosomal translocations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Base excision repair removes single damaged bases and does not repair double-strand breaks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mismatch repair corrects replication mismatches, not double-strand breaks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nonhomologous end joining is error-prone and can introduce mutations and translocations, so this reasoning is incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nucleotide excision repair removes helix-distorting single-strand lesions, not double-strand breaks.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her roommate, who reports that she has been acting bizarrely and had flu-like symptoms a few days earlier. She is admitted, and about a week later she develops unstable blood pressure, fever, involuntary facial movements, and becomes obtunded. Assuming all of these findings are attributable to a single underlying cancer, which of the following malignancies is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis presents with a psychiatric/flu-like prodrome followed by autonomic instability and is most strongly associated with ovarian teratoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is the classic biphasic course of anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis (ANRE): an initial phase dominated by psychiatric symptoms and seizures, followed roughly a week later by decreased consciousness, dyskinesia, and autonomic instability (labile blood pressure, arrhythmia, hyperthermia). ANRE is caused by autoantibodies against NMDA receptors, and the tumor most commonly associated with it is ovarian teratoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastric adenocarcinoma is associated with acanthosis nigricans and the sign of Leser-Trelat, not with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphoma can cause calcitriol-mediated hypercalcemia but is not the tumor linked to anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Small cell lung cancer is linked to many paraneoplastic syndromes but is not the typical tumor behind anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thymoma is associated with myasthenia gravis, not anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is evaluated for progressive weight loss and epigastric pain. On examination, he has thickened, velvety, hyperpigmented plaques over the back of his neck and in both axillae that developed over the past several months. He is not obese and has no history of diabetes. Which of the following malignancies is most likely underlying his skin findings?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung

explanation.summary: Paraneoplastic acanthosis nigricans in a non-obese, non-diabetic adult is most commonly associated with gastric adenocarcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acanthosis nigricans is thickened, black or brown, velvety hyperpigmentation, most commonly on the neck and axilla. Although most cases are linked to obesity or diabetes, roughly 20% are paraneoplastic, and when so, the most commonly associated tumor is gastric adenocarcinoma. These tumors are thought to secrete growth factors that stimulate the characteristic skin changes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ovarian teratoma is associated with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, not acanthosis nigricans.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Small cell lung cancer is associated with LEMS, limbic encephalitis, Cushing syndrome, and SIADH rather than acanthosis nigricans.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is the classic PTHrP-secreting tumor causing hypercalcemia, not acanthosis nigricans.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thymoma is associated with myasthenia gravis, not with paraneoplastic skin hyperpigmentation.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old woman with known breast cancer presents with headache, fatigue, constipation, depression, and forgetfulness. A routine metabolic panel is drawn. Which of the following abnormalities is most likely responsible for her symptoms?

explanation.summary: The constellation of stones, bones, groans, and psychiatric overtones in a cancer patient points to paraneoplastic hypercalcemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Her constipation (groans), depression and forgetfulness (psychiatric overtones), and fatigue are classic manifestations of hypercalcemia. In a patient with malignancy, symptomatic hypercalcemia is most often paraneoplastic, typically driven by tumor secretion of PTHrP. Breast carcinoma is among the carcinomas that cause PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypernatremia is not a paraneoplastic syndrome of breast cancer and typically causes intense thirst and confusion, not this symptom pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypokalemia can cause constipation and weakness, but paralysis would predominate and it is not a feature of paraneoplastic syndromes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hyponatremia is seen in SIADH and causes neurologic findings such as decreased consciousness; it is most associated with small cell lung cancer, not breast cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Isolated hypophosphatemia does not produce this symptom complex; low phosphate accompanies PTHrP-driven hypercalcemia but the calcium elevation drives symptoms.

questions.stem: A man with a 45-pack-year smoking history presents with an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. On history he reports persistent pain in his knees and ankles, and examination reveals digital clubbing with bilateral swelling of the knees and ankles. In addition to treating the exacerbation, evaluation for which of the following conditions is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: New-onset digital clubbing with joint swelling and pain is hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, which is most commonly paraneoplastic and associated with lung cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy is characterized by digital clubbing, synovial effusions, and joint pain, and about 90% of cases are paraneoplastic. Lung cancer of any type is the most commonly associated malignancy, so sudden-onset clubbing should always prompt a work-up for an underlying lung malignancy. The mechanism involves subperiosteal bone formation along the phalanges.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Colon adenocarcinoma may be associated with acanthosis nigricans but not with hypertrophic osteoarthropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gastric adenocarcinoma is linked to acanthosis nigricans and the sign of Leser-Trelat, not hypertrophic osteoarthropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lymphoma may cause calcitriol-mediated hypercalcemia but is not associated with hypertrophic osteoarthropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal cell carcinoma can cause hypercalcemia but is not the tumor behind hypertrophic osteoarthropathy.

questions.stem: Parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP) is most commonly produced by which of the following cancers?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Small cell carcinoma of the lung

choices.label: E
choices.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung

explanation.summary: PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia is most commonly caused by squamous cell carcinoma of the lung.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most malignant tumors that cause hypercalcemia do so by secreting PTHrP, which raises serum calcium and lowers serum phosphate. The cancers most commonly responsible are squamous cell carcinomas of the lung and head and neck, along with carcinomas of the breast, ovary, kidney, and bladder. Of the listed options, squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is the classic PTHrP producer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastric adenocarcinoma is associated with acanthosis nigricans and the sign of Leser-Trelat, not PTHrP production.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphoma can on occasion produce calcitriol, but it is not known to produce PTHrP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ovarian teratoma is associated with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, not PTHrP production.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Small cell lung cancer produces ACTH and ADH (causing Cushing syndrome and SIADH) but is not the typical PTHrP producer.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man reports drooping eyelids and progressive muscle weakness that worsens as the day goes on and with repetitive activity. Imaging reveals an anterior mediastinal mass. His symptoms are attributable to a paraneoplastic process. Antibodies against which of the following are most likely responsible?

choices.label: B
choices.text: NMDA receptors in the central nervous system

explanation.summary: Myasthenia gravis with a thymoma is driven by antibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction targeting postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors, producing weakness that worsens with repetitive use. When paraneoplastic, it is most commonly associated with thymoma (an anterior mediastinal mass), where an immune response against a thymoma epitope cross-reacts with neuromuscular junction components sharing that epitope.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-Hu antibodies mediate limbic encephalitis associated with small cell lung cancer, not myasthenia gravis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibodies to NMDA receptors cause anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, associated with ovarian teratoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibodies against presynaptic calcium channels cause Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, in which weakness improves with use and which is linked to small cell lung cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Voltage-gated potassium channel antibodies are not the mechanism described for this thymoma-associated presentation.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with a long smoking history reports proximal leg weakness that seems to improve slightly after a few minutes of activity. Work-up reveals a lung mass consistent with small cell lung cancer. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology of his weakness?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tumor secretion of parathyroid hormone-related protein

explanation.summary: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome results from antibodies against presynaptic calcium channels and is most commonly associated with small cell lung cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is caused by autoantibodies against presynaptic calcium channels on motor neurons, so patients present with weakness that can improve as the muscle is used. As a paraneoplastic syndrome it is most commonly associated with small cell lung cancer, arising from cross-reactivity between epitopes on the cancer cells and the calcium channels.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibodies to postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors cause myasthenia gravis, in which weakness worsens with use and which is linked to thymoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ectopic ACTH secretion causes paraneoplastic Cushing syndrome, not muscle weakness of this pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ectopic ADH secretion causes SIADH with hyponatremia, not calcium-channel-mediated weakness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PTHrP secretion causes hypercalcemia, not the presynaptic neuromuscular defect of LEMS.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with newly diagnosed small cell lung cancer presents with confusion, malaise, and a seizure. Laboratory studies show a serum sodium of 118 mEq/L, low serum osmolality, and urine that is inappropriately concentrated. Which of the following mechanisms best explains her findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies against the Hu antigen on neurons and tumor cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ectopic production of adrenocorticotropic hormone by the tumor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ectopic production of antidiuretic hormone by the tumor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tumor secretion of calcitriol acting on the intestinal mucosa

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tumor secretion of parathyroid hormone-related protein

explanation.summary: Hyponatremia with low serum osmolality and concentrated urine in small cell lung cancer indicates SIADH from ectopic ADH production.
explanation.whyCorrect: The syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) results from ectopic, unregulated ADH production by the tumor, and small cell lung cancer is by far the most commonly associated cancer. Excess ADH increases water reabsorption in the collecting ducts, producing dilutional hyponatremia (Na <135 mEq/L), hypo-osmolality (<275 mOsm/kg), and urine that is less dilute than expected (>100 mOsm/kg), with neurologic symptoms such as seizures and decreased consciousness.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-Hu antibodies cause limbic encephalitis, a neurologic syndrome, not an electrolyte disturbance.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ectopic ACTH causes Cushing syndrome (hypercortisolism), which does not produce hyponatremia with concentrated urine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Calcitriol secretion causes hypercalcemia (seen with lymphoma), not hyponatremia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PTHrP secretion causes hypercalcemia with low phosphate, not the hyponatremic picture described.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with small cell lung cancer develops central obesity, a rounded plethoric face, a dorsocervical fat pad, and new hyperglycemia. His serum cortisol is markedly elevated. Which of the following best explains the underlying mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoantibodies directed against the adrenal cortical cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ectopic secretion of an ACTH-like substance by the tumor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ectopic secretion of antidiuretic hormone by the tumor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Primary adrenal cortical adenoma independent of the lung tumor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tumor secretion of parathyroid hormone-related protein

explanation.summary: Paraneoplastic Cushing syndrome is caused by tumor secretion of an ACTH-like substance, most commonly by small cell lung cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cushing syndrome from high cortisol produces a dorsocervical fat pad (buffalo hump), moon facies, and hyperglycemia. Although most cases have other causes, a paraneoplastic subset is caused by small cell lung cancer secreting a substance so similar to ACTH that it stimulates cortisol production by the adrenal gland. This ectopic secretion is unresponsive to normal feedback inhibition.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoantibodies against adrenal cells would reduce, not increase, cortisol and are not the paraneoplastic mechanism described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ectopic ADH causes SIADH with hyponatremia, not Cushing syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A primary adrenal adenoma is not a paraneoplastic syndrome and does not fit the setting of a known small cell lung cancer secreting an ACTH-like substance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PTHrP secretion causes hypercalcemia, not hypercortisolism.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with a heavy smoking history develops the subacute onset of short-term memory loss, seizures, personality changes, and olfactory hallucinations. MRI shows inflammation of the medial temporal lobes. Antibodies against which of the following are most characteristically implicated, and with which tumor is this syndrome most associated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anti-Hu antigen; small cell lung cancer

choices.label: D
choices.text: Presynaptic calcium channels; small cell lung cancer

choices.label: E
choices.text: PTHrP; squamous cell carcinoma of the lung

explanation.summary: Paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis presents with short-term memory loss and seizures, involves anti-Hu antibodies, and is most associated with small cell lung cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Limbic encephalitis is an immune-mediated inflammation of the limbic system with subacute short-term memory loss (a hallmark), seizures, personality changes, and olfactory/gustatory hallucinations. The most commonly associated cancer is small cell lung cancer, and antibodies against the neuronal antigen Hu (anti-Hu antibodies) play an important role.

whyWrongByChoice.B: NMDA receptor antibodies and ovarian teratoma define anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, which has a psychiatric prodrome and autonomic instability rather than isolated limbic memory loss.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor antibodies with thymoma cause myasthenia gravis, a neuromuscular junction disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Presynaptic calcium channel antibodies cause Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (muscle weakness), not limbic encephalitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PTHrP from squamous cell carcinoma causes hypercalcemia, not an encephalitis.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man is noted to have the abrupt appearance of numerous gray-brown, flat-topped, velvety, stuck-on-appearing skin lesions across his trunk over a few weeks. Work-up is initiated for an underlying malignancy. This sign is most commonly associated with which cancer, and which secreted mediator is thought to drive the lesions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma; transforming growth factor alpha

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ovarian teratoma; antibodies against the NMDA receptor subunit

choices.label: C
choices.text: Small cell lung cancer; ectopic antidiuretic hormone secretion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung; parathyroid hormone-related protein

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thymoma; antibodies against the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor

explanation.summary: The sign of Leser-Trelat is a sudden eruption of seborrheic keratoses associated with GI adenocarcinoma and driven by tumor secretion of TGF-alpha.
explanation.whyCorrect: The sign of Leser-Trelat is the sudden, explosive appearance of numerous seborrheic keratoses, which are gray-brown, flat-topped, velvety lesions with a stuck-on appearance. When they appear suddenly in large numbers, an underlying malignancy should be sought; the most commonly associated cancers involve the gastrointestinal tract. These tumors secrete transforming growth factor alpha, which stimulates keratinocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ovarian teratoma and NMDA receptor antibodies cause anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, not seborrheic keratoses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Small cell lung cancer and ADH cause SIADH, not seborrheic keratoses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Squamous cell carcinoma and PTHrP cause hypercalcemia, not the sign of Leser-Trelat.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thymoma and acetylcholine receptor antibodies cause myasthenia gravis, not a cutaneous eruption.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with lymphoma is found to have hypercalcemia. Unlike the more common paraneoplastic mechanism, laboratory studies show that both serum calcium and serum phosphate are elevated. Which of the following secreted substances best explains this finding?

explanation.summary: Calcitriol-mediated hypercalcemia raises both calcium and phosphate and is seen primarily in lymphoma, distinguishing it from PTHrP-driven hypercalcemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although most paraneoplastic hypercalcemia is driven by PTHrP (which raises calcium but lowers phosphate), malignant tumors can also cause hypercalcemia by secreting calcitriol, the active form of vitamin D. Calcitriol ultimately increases both serum calcium and serum phosphate. This less common mechanism is seen primarily in patients with lymphoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ACTH causes Cushing syndrome via cortisol, not hypercalcemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ADH causes SIADH with hyponatremia, not hypercalcemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PTHrP raises calcium but decreases phosphate, so it does not explain the elevated phosphate seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transforming growth factor alpha drives the sign of Leser-Trelat, not calcium elevation.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with a 40 pack-year smoking history presents with hemoptysis and weight loss, and imaging reveals a spiculated lung mass. Setting his individual case aside, which of the following cancers is the leading cause of cancer-related death in both men and women in the United States?

explanation.summary: Lung cancer is the number one cause of cancer mortality in both sexes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although breast (women) and prostate (men) cancers have higher incidence, lung cancer has a poor prognosis and causes the most cancer deaths in both men and women. Many of these deaths are preventable by avoiding tobacco smoke.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in women but is the second most common cause of cancer death in women, not the first.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Colorectal cancer is a common cancer but ranks below lung cancer as a cause of cancer death.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pancreatic cancer is uncommon and highly lethal, but its total number of deaths is far below that of lung cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in men but has a relatively good prognosis and is not the leading cause of cancer death.

questions.stem: In the United States, both the incidence of and mortality from cervical cancer decreased by more than 60% between 1955 and 1992. Which of the following interventions is most responsible for this dramatic decline?

explanation.summary: Cervical cancer rates fell largely because of Pap smear screening.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Papanicolaou (Pap) test, introduced in the 1950s, allows cytologic detection of precancerous cervical lesions before invasive cancer develops. Its widespread use is credited with the >60% decline in cervical cancer incidence and mortality in the US during this period.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Low-dose chest CT is used for lung cancer screening and is unrelated to cervical cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fecal occult blood testing screens for colorectal cancer, not cervical cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Colonoscopy screens for colorectal cancer and has no role in cervical cancer prevention.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mammography is a screening test for breast cancer, not cervical cancer.

questions.stem: A healthy 45-year-old man with no personal or family history of cancer or cancer syndromes presents to establish care and asks about cancer screening. At what age is initiation of colorectal cancer screening routinely recommended for an average-risk individual such as this patient?

explanation.summary: Average-risk colorectal cancer screening begins at age 45.
explanation.whyCorrect: For healthy individuals without a family history or cancer syndrome, colonoscopy screening is recommended beginning at age 45 and is repeated every 10 years. Colonoscopy is the gold standard because it visualizes the colon and removes polyps before they can progress to cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Age 21 is when average-risk women typically begin Pap smear (cervical cancer) screening, not colorectal screening.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Age 30 is when high-risk BRCA1/2 carriers may begin breast MRI screening, not colorectal screening.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Age 40 applies to patients with a family history of colorectal adenocarcinoma (or 10 years before the affected relative's onset), not to average-risk patients.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Because most cancers occur in patients over 55 years of age, beginning routine screening at 65 would miss many preventable cancers.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man who worked for decades installing insulation and demolishing old buildings presents with dyspnea and chest pain. Imaging shows diffuse pleural thickening, and pleural biopsy reveals a malignant tumor. Occupational exposure to which of the following is most likely responsible for his cancer?

explanation.summary: Asbestos exposure from construction materials causes mesothelioma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Asbestos, encountered in construction materials, is the classic occupational carcinogen linked to mesothelioma, a pleural-based malignancy. This patient's demolition and insulation work is a typical high-exposure history.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Benzene, found in printing, paint, and light oil, is linked to acute myeloid leukemia, not mesothelioma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Radon, encountered in underground mines and some homes, is linked to lung cancer rather than pleural mesothelioma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ultraviolet radiation causes skin cancers such as melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma, not mesothelioma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vinyl chloride, used in refrigerants and adhesives, is linked to hepatic angiosarcoma.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man who has worked in a printing and paint manufacturing plant for many years presents with fatigue and easy bruising. His blood counts show pancytopenia, and bone marrow evaluation confirms acute myeloid leukemia. Chronic occupational exposure to which of the following agents is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: Benzene exposure is linked to acute myeloid leukemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Benzene is encountered in printing, paint, and light oil and is a well-recognized occupational carcinogen linked to acute myeloid leukemia. This patient's plant work fits the classic exposure history.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aromatic amines are not the occupational agent emphasized here; the printing and paint setting points specifically to benzene and acute myeloid leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Asbestos, from construction materials, is linked to mesothelioma, not leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Radon, from underground mines and some residences, is linked to lung cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vinyl chloride, from refrigerants and adhesives, is linked to hepatic angiosarcoma.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man who worked for years manufacturing PVC pipe presents with right upper quadrant pain. Imaging reveals a vascular hepatic tumor, and biopsy confirms a malignant tumor of endothelial origin in the liver. Occupational exposure to which of the following is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Vinyl chloride exposure causes hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vinyl chloride, used in refrigerants and adhesives, is the occupational carcinogen linked to hepatic angiosarcoma, a malignant vascular (endothelial) tumor of the liver. This patient's PVC manufacturing work is the classic exposure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aflatoxin is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma, not the endothelial hepatic angiosarcoma described, and is not the occupational agent emphasized in this brick.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Asbestos is linked to mesothelioma, a pleural tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Benzene is linked to acute myeloid leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Radon is linked to lung cancer, not a hepatic vascular tumor.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman is diagnosed with luminal (hormone receptor-positive) breast cancer. In counseling her, you note that increased lifetime estrogen exposure is an important risk factor for this cancer. Which of the following features in her history most likely increased her estrogen exposure and her breast cancer risk?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Having given birth to five children

explanation.summary: Early menarche increases lifetime estrogen exposure and breast cancer risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Estrogen stimulates growth and epithelial proliferation in luminal breast cancer. Risk factors that increase estrogen exposure include menarche before age 12, delayed first childbirth after 30 or nulliparity, supplemental estrogen, and postmenopausal obesity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Postmenopausal obesity, not being underweight, is the estrogen-related risk factor for breast cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Early menopause shortens the reproductive window and reduces lifetime estrogen exposure, lowering risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An early first full-term pregnancy is protective, whereas delaying first childbirth past age 30 raises risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Higher parity (more pregnancies) reduces lifetime estrogen exposure because progesterone counterbalances estrogen during pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with a long history of chronic gastritis undergoes endoscopy. Biopsies show gastric adenocarcinoma in one region and a mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma in another. Which of the following infectious agents is most likely causally related to both of these neoplasms?

explanation.summary: H. pylori is causally linked to gastric carcinoma and MALT lymphoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although viruses cause most infection-related cancers, Helicobacter pylori is a well-researched bacterial example that is causally related to both gastric carcinoma and MALT lymphoma. Infectious agents cause roughly 15% of cancers worldwide.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Epstein-Barr virus is not the agent emphasized here; the gastric carcinoma plus MALT lymphoma combination points specifically to H. pylori.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatitis viruses may cause hepatocellular carcinoma, not the gastric tumors described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Human herpesvirus 8 is associated with Kaposi sarcoma, not gastric cancer or MALT lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HPV causes cervical cancer, not gastric carcinoma or MALT lymphoma.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man who drinks alcohol heavily and smokes a pack of cigarettes daily presents with progressive dysphagia and weight loss. Endoscopy reveals an esophageal mass, and biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma. His combination of exposures is best described as having what effect on his cancer risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alcohol and tobacco act synergistically to increase risk

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alcohol protects against the carcinogenic effect of tobacco

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither exposure affects the risk of esophageal cancer

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only alcohol contributes; tobacco is not a risk factor for this cancer

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only tobacco contributes; alcohol is not a risk factor for this cancer

explanation.summary: Alcohol and tobacco act synergistically to raise the risk of aerodigestive cancers.
explanation.whyCorrect: Excessive alcohol increases the risk of cancers of the mouth, larynx, and esophagus, and when the patient is also a smoker, the risk is synergistically increased. Both exposures are independent risk factors whose combined effect is greater than additive.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Alcohol does not protect against tobacco; it amplifies the carcinogenic risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both alcohol and tobacco clearly increase esophageal cancer risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tobacco is a major risk factor for esophageal cancer, so alcohol is not the only contributor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alcohol is itself an established risk factor for esophageal cancer, so tobacco is not the only contributor.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with a strong family history of colon cancer undergoes colonoscopy, which reveals hundreds of adenomatous polyps carpeting the colon. He is told that without intervention his lifetime risk of colorectal adenocarcinoma approaches 100%. A germline mutation in which of the following genes is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: Familial adenomatous polyposis is caused by a germline APC mutation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Familial adenomatosis polyposis syndrome carries a nearly 100% chance of colorectal adenocarcinoma and is due to a germline mutation in the APC tumor suppressor gene. The hundreds of adenomas and near-certain cancer risk are classic.

whyWrongByChoice.B: BRCA1 mutations predispose to breast and ovarian carcinoma, not colonic polyposis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NF1 mutations cause neurofibromatosis 1, characterized by neurofibromas and cafe-au-lait macules.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RB1 mutations cause retinoblastoma tumor predisposition syndrome, not colonic polyposis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TP53 germline mutations cause Li-Fraumeni syndrome, associated with breast cancer and other tumors.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with a family history of breast and ovarian cancer diagnosed before age 50 is found to carry a germline BRCA1 mutation. She is counseled about intensified screening, including breast MRI before age 30 and consideration of prophylactic mastectomy. The BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes normally function to prevent cancer by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Encoding a growth-factor receptor tyrosine kinase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maintaining DNA repair and genomic stability

choices.label: E
choices.text: Producing estrogen to regulate epithelial growth

explanation.summary: BRCA1/2 are DNA-repair genes; their loss causes genomic instability and cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: BRCA1 and BRCA2 are important to DNA repair, and their absence creates genomic instability that can lead to cancer. Because carriers are high-risk, experts recommend MRI screening before age 30 and some choose prophylactic mastectomy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Although they repair DNA broadly, their described role is genomic stability, not selective repair of UV-damaged skin cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: BRCA1/2 are DNA-repair genes, not growth-factor receptor tyrosine kinases.
whyWrongByChoice.C: They do not detoxify chemical carcinogens; their role is genome maintenance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: BRCA genes do not produce estrogen; estrogen exposure is a separate risk factor for breast cancer.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is evaluated for multiple flat, hyperpigmented (cafe-au-lait) skin macules and several soft cutaneous nodules that on biopsy are neurofibromas. He is diagnosed with an inherited tumor predisposition syndrome. A germline mutation in which of the following tumor suppressor genes is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is caused by inherited NF1 mutations.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neurofibromatosis 1 is caused by inherited mutations in the NF1 tumor suppressor gene and manifests with cafe-au-lait macules and multiple neurofibromas, exactly as described in this child.

whyWrongByChoice.A: APC mutations cause familial adenomatous polyposis with colorectal adenocarcinoma, not neurofibromas.
whyWrongByChoice.B: BRCA2 mutations predispose to breast and ovarian carcinoma, not neurofibromatosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RB1 mutations cause retinoblastoma, a childhood eye tumor, not cafe-au-lait macules and neurofibromas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TP53 mutations cause Li-Fraumeni syndrome, associated with breast and other cancers.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy whose family recently emigrated from Uganda is brought to clinic with a rapidly enlarging mass of the mandible. Biopsy shows sheets of monomorphic, mitotically active B cells with interspersed tingible body macrophages producing a "starry sky" appearance. Which of the following pathogens is most strongly associated with this child's tumor?

explanation.summary: Endemic Burkitt lymphoma classically presents as a pediatric jaw mass in Africa and is strongly associated with EBV.
explanation.whyCorrect: The African (endemic) subtype of Burkitt lymphoma typically presents in children as a large mandibular mass and is virtually always EBV-positive (EBV identified in >90% of endemic cases). The "starry sky" histology of neoplastic B cells with tingible body macrophages is characteristic.

whyWrongByChoice.B: H. pylori is associated with gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma of the stomach, not a pediatric jaw mass.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HPV causes squamous lesions such as warts and squamous cell carcinomas, not Burkitt lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, a malignancy of CD4+ T cells, not a B-cell jaw tumor in children.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. haematobium is associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder, not lymphoma.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man reports abdominal pain after meals, nausea, frequent burping, and unintentional weight loss. Testing confirms infection with a curved gram-negative rod that, if left untreated, can progress to gastric cancer. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which this organism promotes neoplastic transformation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Altered regulation of vascular endothelial growth factor

explanation.summary: H. pylori drives gastric carcinogenesis through longstanding chronic inflammation of the mucosa.
explanation.whyCorrect: Conflict between H. pylori and the host immune system produces chronic gastritis; this longstanding inflammatory damage and resultant epithelial proliferation lead to a step-wise cascade toward gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Altered VEGF regulation is the mechanism of HHV-8 in Kaposi sarcoma, not of H. pylori.
whyWrongByChoice.C: E6 inactivation of p53 is a mechanism of high-risk HPV, not H. pylori.
whyWrongByChoice.D: E7 inactivation of Rb is a mechanism of high-risk HPV, not H. pylori.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The Tax oncoprotein is implicated in HTLV-1-driven adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma.

questions.stem: A pathologist reviews sequential gastric biopsies from a patient with chronic H. pylori infection to document the precancerous cascade. Which of the following histologic changes occurs immediately before the development of invasive gastric adenocarcinoma?

explanation.summary: Dysplasia is the pre-malignant step that directly precedes invasive gastric adenocarcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the H. pylori cascade, chronic gastritis leads to atrophic gastritis, then intestinal metaplasia, then dysplasia (enlarged, hyperchromatic, crowded nuclei). When dysplastic cells invade surrounding tissue, invasive gastric adenocarcinoma is formed, so dysplasia is the last step before invasion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atrophic gastritis occurs earlier in the cascade, before intestinal metaplasia and dysplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperplasia is not the identified step in this cascade and does not directly precede invasion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypertrophy is not a step described in the gastric precancerous cascade.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intestinal metaplasia (goblet and Paneth cells) precedes dysplasia, not invasion directly.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has an abnormal Pap smear, and cervical biopsy reveals non-keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma. The lesion is driven by a virus that produces two oncoproteins not made by low-risk serotypes. Which of the following best describes the action of these oncoproteins?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They inactivate p53 and Rb, removing the G1-to-S checkpoint

choices.label: B
choices.text: They incorporate viral DNA directly into the hepatocyte genome

choices.label: C
choices.text: They inhibit apoptosis while driving CD4+ T-cell proliferation

choices.label: D
choices.text: They stimulate transcription of viral RNA to expand T cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: They upregulate VEGF to promote angiogenesis

explanation.summary: High-risk HPV E6 and E7 oncoproteins inactivate p53 and Rb, permitting uncontrolled proliferation.
explanation.whyCorrect: High-risk HPV serotypes (16, 18, 31, 33) produce E6 and E7 oncoproteins. E6 inactivates p53 and E7 inactivates Rb; without normal p53 and Rb function the cell cycle proceeds through the G1-to-S transition unchecked, permitting uncontrolled proliferation that, with accumulated mutations, progresses to carcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Incorporation of viral DNA into hepatocytes describes HBV, not HPV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibiting apoptosis while driving CD4+ T-cell proliferation describes the HTLV-1 HBZ protein.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stimulating transcription of viral RNA to expand T cells describes the HTLV-1 Tax protein.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VEGF upregulation and angiogenesis is the HHV-8/Kaposi sarcoma mechanism.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man receiving antiretroviral therapy for HIV presents with multiple red-violet, raised plaques on his arms that continue to grow. Biopsy shows a proliferation of neoplastic vascular channels. The causative virus promotes this tumor primarily by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding of the CD21 surface marker on resting B lymphocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic inflammation of the bladder urothelial epithelium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inactivation of p53 by the E6 oncoprotein of the virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Integration of viral DNA into the host hepatocyte genome

explanation.summary: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma by deregulating VEGF, driving angiogenesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8, which alters regulation of VEGF. VEGF drives angiogenesis, and its continuous activation leads to proliferating mesenchymal/endothelial cells that form a vascular sarcoma, appearing as red-violet skin lesions, especially in immunosuppressed patients with AIDS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD21 binding on B lymphocytes describes EBV, not HHV-8.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic bladder inflammation describes Schistosoma haematobium, not HHV-8.
whyWrongByChoice.D: E6 inactivation of p53 is a high-risk HPV mechanism, not HHV-8.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Integration of viral DNA into hepatocytes describes HBV in hepatocellular carcinoma.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man presents with painless, enlarging cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Lymph node biopsy shows large malignant cells with a bilobed nucleus and prominent eosinophilic nucleoli described as "owl eye" cells. Which of the following viruses is most commonly associated with this malignancy?

explanation.summary: Reed-Sternberg 'owl eye' cells indicate classic Hodgkin lymphoma, ~50% of which are EBV-associated.
explanation.whyCorrect: The bilobed "owl eye" Reed-Sternberg cell is the key histologic finding of classic Hodgkin lymphoma, which typically presents with painless supradiaphragmatic lymphadenopathy. Approximately 50% of classic Hodgkin lymphoma cases are related to EBV infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HBV is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma, not Hodgkin lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HCV is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma, not Reed-Sternberg cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HPV causes squamous lesions and carcinomas, not Hodgkin lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, which shows a flower-shaped nucleus, not owl eye cells.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man from southern Japan develops fatigue, hypercalcemia, and lymphadenopathy. A peripheral smear shows malignant CD4+ T cells, some with a characteristic multi-lobated, flower-shaped nucleus. Which of the following viruses is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: A flower-shaped nucleus in a malignancy of CD4+ T cells signals HTLV-1-associated adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: HTLV-1 is a retrovirus endemic to regions including Japan that shows tropism for CD4+ T cells. It causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL); in the acute phase, a characteristic multi-lobated, flower-shaped nucleus may be seen. Neoplastic transformation is linked to the viral Tax and HBZ proteins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: EBV is associated with Hodgkin lymphoma, Burkitt lymphoma, and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not the flower cell.
whyWrongByChoice.B: H. pylori is a bacterium associated with gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma, not ATLL.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma and primary effusion lymphoma, not ATLL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HPV causes squamous lesions and carcinomas, not a T-cell leukemia.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use has chronic hepatitis progressing to cirrhosis. Imaging reveals a liver mass, and biopsy shows plump, eosinophilic polygonal cells with nuclear atypia that resemble hepatocytes. Which of the following best explains the development of this malignancy?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tropism of the virus for CD4+ T cells

explanation.summary: Chronic HCV (or HBV) infection causes hepatocellular carcinoma through longstanding inflammatory damage and cirrhosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: HCV is transmitted commonly by IV drug use, and about 60-80% of infections become chronic. Long-term inflammation and cellular injury evolve to cirrhosis and damage cellular DNA, with reactive oxygen species and increased hepatocyte proliferation, resulting in hepatocellular carcinoma composed of plump, eosinophilic malignant hepatocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bacterial-driven intestinal metaplasia describes H. pylori in the stomach, not HCV in the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.B: VEGF deregulation is the HHV-8/Kaposi sarcoma mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: E7 inactivation of Rb is a high-risk HPV mechanism, not a hepatitis virus mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tropism for CD4+ T cells describes HTLV-1, not a hepatitis virus.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man who spent years in North Africa presents with painless hematuria. Cystoscopy shows a bladder mass, and biopsy reveals squamous cell carcinoma with adjacent parasitic eggs bearing a terminal spine. Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: S. haematobium has an affinity for the bladder and causes squamous cell carcinoma via chronic inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Schistosoma haematobium is a parasitic flatworm that has an affinity for the bladder, where it causes urinary schistosomiasis. Cyclical infection and immune response drive chronic inflammation and reactive oxygen species that damage DNA; over time the bladder epithelium undergoes metaplasia, dysplasia, and finally squamous cell carcinoma. Its eggs are recognized by a terminal spine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: EBV is associated with lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not bladder cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: H. pylori affects the stomach (adenocarcinoma, MALT lymphoma), not the bladder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HBV causes hepatocellular carcinoma, not bladder squamous cell carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: While HPV causes squamous carcinomas at other sites, the parasitic eggs with a terminal spine identify Schistosoma.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman has epigastric discomfort, and gastric biopsy shows an increased population of small, neoplastic B cells consistent with extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue. Testing is positive for H. pylori. Which of the following statements about her condition is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A substantial proportion of cases are cured by antibiotic eradication of the infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: The lesion characteristically shows binucleate Reed-Sternberg cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: The malignant cells are CD4+ T cells with multi-lobated nuclei

choices.label: D
choices.text: The tumor arises from neoplastic vascular endothelial channels driven by HHV-8

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tumor is driven by the E6 and E7 oncoproteins of high-risk HPV

explanation.summary: Gastric MALT lymphoma is H. pylori-associated, and many cases regress after antibiotic eradication.
explanation.whyCorrect: Extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma of the stomach is associated with H. pylori infection secondary to chronic bacterial-driven immune stimulation. Histology shows an increased population of small neoplastic B cells, and a substantial proportion of H. pylori-associated MALT lymphoma cases are cured following H. pylori eradication with antibiotics.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Reed-Sternberg cells characterize Hodgkin lymphoma, not MALT lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MALT lymphoma is a B-cell neoplasm; CD4+ T-cell malignancy describes HTLV-1-associated ATLL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neoplastic vascular channels describe Kaposi sarcoma, not MALT lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: E6 and E7 oncoproteins drive high-risk HPV carcinomas, not gastric MALT lymphoma.

questions.stem: A pediatric oncologist confirms Burkitt lymphoma in a young patient, noting a highly proliferative B-cell tumor. Which of the following chromosomal translocations is classically associated with this lymphoma?

explanation.summary: Burkitt lymphoma is classically driven by the t(8;14) translocation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Burkitt lymphoma is a highly mitotically active non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma classically associated with the t(8;14) translocation, which places the MYC oncogene under the influence of the immunoglobulin heavy-chain promoter, driving the aggressive proliferation seen on the "starry sky" histology.

whyWrongByChoice.B: t(9;22), the Philadelphia chromosome, is associated with chronic myeloid leukemia, not Burkitt lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: t(11;22) is associated with Ewing sarcoma, not Burkitt lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: t(14;18) is associated with follicular lymphoma (BCL2), not Burkitt lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: t(15;17) is associated with acute promyelocytic leukemia, not Burkitt lymphoma.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old sexually active man presents with soft, cauliflower-like growths on the genitals. Biopsy shows a benign papillary proliferation of squamous epithelium without invasion. Which of the following HPV serotypes are most likely responsible for these lesions?

explanation.summary: Low-risk HPV serotypes 6 and 11 cause genital warts (condyloma acuminata) that do not commonly progress to cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Low-risk HPV serotypes 6 and 11 cause genital warts (condyloma acuminata) and squamous papillomas of the larynx (laryngeal papillomatosis). These are composed of a benign papillary proliferation of squamous epithelium and do not commonly progress to cancer because they do not produce the E6 and E7 oncoproteins.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk serotypes that produce E6/E7 and cause squamous cell carcinomas, not benign genital warts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HPV 16 and 31 are both high-risk carcinogenic serotypes, not the cause of benign genital warts.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HPV 18 and 33 are both high-risk carcinogenic serotypes, not the cause of benign genital warts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HPV 31 and 33 are high-risk serotypes associated with carcinoma, not benign condyloma acuminata.
